## Summary

At a university Q&A recorded October 29 and published December 1, 2025, Eisman explains the financial crisis through leverage, bad underwriting, concentrated ownership and interconnected derivatives. He favors US equities and continued AI spending, expects bank consolidation, and explicitly withholds an opinion on private-credit insurance risk. The historical credit framework is useful; several absolute claims about regulation, investigations and financing need qualification.

The strongest material explanation is the interaction of credit deterioration, leverage and funding. His stated uncertainty on private credit is preserved rather than rewritten as a bearish forecast. Regulatory and due-diligence simplifications are weaker, and an optimistic AI-spending scenario is not an unconditional market target.

### 001. Sell-side analysts can favor management access and avoid negative recommendations because client access helps their business.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 6:44-7:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=404s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The incentive explanation is plausible, but this episode offers no representative evidence for its claim about most analysts.

Assessment test: Compare analyst recommendations, access arrangements and documented restrictions across a defined sample.

Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

### 005. Gross leverage at major financial institutions tripled between 1997 and 2007 while risk-weighted leverage stayed flat.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 14:25-15:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=865s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The precise universe, balance-sheet definition and endpoints are unspecified. Primary data show substantial variation across firms; the blanket multiple is not established.

Assessment test: Reconstruct consistent 1997 and 2007 gross and risk-weighted ratios for the named universe.

### 008. Buying credit protection reduces exposure to the borrower but creates dependence on the protection seller surviving when payment is due.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 17:14-19:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=1034s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Conditional reasoning: The promised payment is valuable only to the extent the protection seller or pledged collateral can satisfy it.

Assessment test: Identify the protection obligation, collateral and counterparty resources.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c015"></a>
### 015. Post-crisis regulation and stress testing materially increased bank resilience by increasing capital and reducing risky exposures.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

The Fed confirms a substantial post-crisis capital increase. Exact claims about leverage being more than halved everywhere are not independently resolved.

- [2025 stress test background](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-june-dodd-frank-act-stress-test-background.htm) (2025-06-27): Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c017"></a>
### 017. SVB essentially just took venture deposits and bought long-term Treasuries; that was its business.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 30:22-31:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=1822s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The description is materially oversimplified. An inspected supervisory account establishes securities and interest-rate exposure, but this review has not yet attached the full asset table needed for a definitive composition grade.

- [Review of SVB supervision: key takeaways](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2023-April-SVB-Key-Takeaways.htm) (2023-04-28): Concentrated uninsured deposits, interest-rate risk and weak liquidity management left SVB vulnerable; the securities sale and proposed capital raise preceded a run exceeding $40 billion on March 9.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c020"></a>
### 020. There are essentially no newly underwritten subprime mortgages in the United States.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 33:11-33:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=1991s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

He softens the literal zero, but does not define subprime as borrower credit quality, product structure or private securitization. Modern low-score government-insured loans are not equivalent to pre-crisis subprime products.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c021"></a>
### 021. He knows of no mortgage-underwriting regulation; the real constraint is the bank stress test.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 33:24-33:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=2004s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Covered mortgage lenders have an explicit ability-to-repay duty under Regulation Z. Stress tests are important but cannot substitute for this underwriting regime.

Qualification: He qualifies the first clause as his knowledge, but presents it as the explanation of the regulatory constraint.

Assessment test: Inspect applicable underwriting rules and the population subject to stress tests.

- [Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage final rule](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/final-rules/ability-repay-and-qualified-mortgage-standards-under-truth-lending-act-regulation-z/) (2013-01-10): Covered mortgage creditors must make a reasonable, good-faith ability-to-repay determination. Mortgage underwriting rules exist independently of bank stress tests.
- [2025 stress test background](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-june-dodd-frank-act-stress-test-background.htm) (2025-06-27): Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

### 022. Technology and compliance costs favor scale, and regional-bank consolidation should accelerate.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c028"></a>
### 028. In the simplified waterfall, three 3% layers are exhausted when cumulative pool losses reach 9%.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 43:30-44:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=2610s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The arithmetic is correct under the stated sequential-loss structure; real transactions also involve cash flows, triggers and recoveries.

Conditional reasoning: 3% + 3% + 3% = 9%; the third layer is fully impaired at that cumulative loss.

Assessment test: Apply loss allocation to the stated example.


<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c029"></a>
### 029. Due-diligence samples revealed deficient mortgages, yet securitizations proceeded with inadequate disclosure of loan quality.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 45:31-49:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=2731s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The FCIC documents sampled failures, waivers and disclosure problems. The account should not be read as proof that every firm followed an identical sample size and procedure.

Assessment test: Compare Clayton results, waivers and investor disclosures.

- [FCIC report, Clayton due diligence findings, printed pp.165-169](https://fcic-static.law.stanford.edu/cdn_media/fcic-reports/fcic_final_report_full.pdf#page=193) (2011-01-27): Clayton rejected 28% of sampled loans; banks waived in 39% of those rejected. Samples and disclosure practices varied; the findings support a serious due-diligence failure but not every universal statement about every firm.

<a id="youtube-m4LSNYEid_g-c030"></a>
### 030. As far as anyone knows, DOJ never even investigated the mortgage due-diligence conduct referred after the crisis inquiry.

DOJ documents investigations and civil resolutions concerning RMBS misconduct. That contradicts a broad impression of no investigation, but does not establish the disposition of every particular FCIC criminal referral.

### 035. AI-investment returns may not be clear until 2027; continued capex expansion keeps the current market story alive.

[Source at 53:18-53:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4LSNYEid_g&t=3198s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: 2027

Assessment test: Revisit realized utilization, revenue, capex and free cash flow through 2027.

A meaningful hedge test must specify regime, asset and horizon. The episode supplies no current correlation calculation, and a long-run debasement thesis does not imply an inverse relationship on every daily move.

Assessment test: Calculate dated rolling correlations and stress-period returns; distinguish inflation shocks from monetary debasement.


## Framework and tools

- Study the debt and funding structure behind equity narratives.
- Look for a shared hidden assumption, such as permanently rising house prices.
- Refresh conviction with recurring operating or loan-vintage data.
- Choose an instrument whose carrying cost lets the thesis survive.
- Say when the available data do not support an opinion.
- Distinguish a sound business or technology from a good investment at the prevailing price.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Risk-weighted assets versus gross leverage
- Mortgage securitization vintage performance
- CDS premiums and counterparty exposure
- Tranche attachment and loss waterfalls
- Bank stress tests and capital ratios
- Capex guidance and corporate cash flow
- Visa spending and bank credit-quality results
- Crypto-equity correlation

## Source cautions

Eisman is the main respondent. Ivy Zelman hosts; students ask questions. Student premises are not assigned to Eisman unless he explicitly adopts them.
- The introduction dates the event October 29, 2025, although this video was published December 1. Statements about current conditions refer to the recording.
- Captions garble company names including Comerica and New Century; obvious names were corrected from context.
- The risk-weighted leverage and mortgage examples are simplified, not calibrated models.
- Opening montage repeats later passages; ads, personal biography, movie anecdotes and career advice are excluded from material-claim counts.
